chief_complaint: low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he picked up a stubborn viral cough that has been going around his office and settled deep in his chest.
concerns: He is worried that coughing non-stop will disrupt his client presentations next week and jeopardize an important project.
expectations: He hopes to get a strong prescription cough suppressant and a medical note excusing him from speaking at meetings for a few days.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Atypical Pneumonia is essential for appropriate diagnostic workup and treatment.
Clinical history, severity assessment, and targeted testing must be interpreted together rather than relying on one symptom alone.
Assess severity, oxygenation, and chest imaging when pneumonia is suspected.
Management should follow local pathways and account for patient-specific comorbidity and clinical severity.
diagnostic_clues: Chief complaint: low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing

Key HPI features: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/examination findings: Perform focused examination, vital-sign assessment, and diagnosis-specific investigations.
common_misconceptions: Assuming a mild or atypical presentation rules out Atypical Pneumonia.
Relying on a single normal test result to prematurely exclude serious pathology.
Equating transient symptom improvement with resolution of the underlying condition.
Failing to consider clinically important alternative diagnoses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before appropriate assessment.
Starting treatment without considering contraindications, interactions, or organ function.
Ignoring critical warning signs: Hypoxaemia or severe dyspnoea.
management_principles: Assess severity, oxygenation, and chest imaging when pneumonia is suspected.
Use local antimicrobial guidance after considering likely pathogens and patient-specific risk factors.
Escalate urgently for hypoxaemia, haemodynamic instability, or worsening respiratory distress.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing

A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with low-grade fever, dry hacking cough, and diffuse wheezing. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain full vital signs including oxygen saturation and a focused respiratory examination; use chest imaging or pathogen testing selectively when it will change management or severity is uncertain.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute respiratory illness; atypical pneumonia is possible, but viral bronchitis and asthma/reactive airways disease remain important alternatives pending examination and investigations.
reference_soap.plan: Assess oxygenation and illness severity before deciding on outpatient care. Provide supportive care and safety-net instructions. If bacterial pneumonia is clinically diagnosed, select antimicrobial treatment under local guidance after checking allergies, pregnancy potential, interacting medicines, and individual risk factors; antibiotics are not routine for uncomplicated viral bronchitis. Arrange urgent emergency assessment for hypoxaemia, severe dyspnoea, confusion, hypotension, chest pain, or clinical deterioration.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Atypical Pneumonia
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Atypical Pneumonia
Implement severity-based evaluation, supportive care, and clinician-directed antimicrobial treatment only when bacterial pneumonia is diagnosed

teaching.one_liner: Lower respiratory infection with a predominantly dry cough and diffuse respiratory symptoms, often caused by atypical organisms.

must_ask.objective: Low-grade fever and dry cough characteristics
must_ask.say: Is your cough dry, and how high has your fever been?
Have you had headache, sore throat, muscle aches, or an upset stomach with this?
Do you live in a dormitory, shared housing, or have close contact with a lot of people, like at school or work?
Has the wheeze been getting gradually worse over days rather than coming on suddenly?

must_ask.objective: Response to prior antibiotics if any
must_ask.say: Have you tried any antibiotics already, and did they help?

history.answer: I have had this dry, hacking cough and a low-grade fever that started about a week ago, and it has just been getting worse.
The cough started about seven days ago and has steadily grown more persistent each day.
It started gradually like a mild scratchy throat and tiredness, and I have never had an illness like this before.
It is almost completely dry and hacking, with only an occasional speck of clear mucus.
It bothers me throughout the whole day, though the coughing fits disrupt my sleep at night.
I get nagging bouts of coughing, but I do not make a whooping noise when breathing in, and I have not vomited from coughing.
Talking for a long time or taking a deep breath triggers a fit, but cold air, dust, or animals do not set it off.
I hear a faint wheezing whistle when I breathe out, and I feel a little winded walking up stairs, but I am not gasping at rest.
My forehead has felt warm with mild chills for the last few days, and my thermometer at home showed around thirty-seven point eight.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I have not had drenching night sweats.
My chest muscles feel sore and tired from coughing so much, but there is no sharp stabbing pain when I take a breath.
I do not have a runny nose, nasal congestion, or any sensation of mucus dripping down the back of my throat.
No, I do not get any heartburn, sour fluid in my mouth, or food coming back up.
No, I have no shortness of breath when lying flat, and my feet and ankles are not swollen.
No, I do not take blood pressure medications or any ACE inhibitors.
I have never smoked cigarettes, e-cigarettes, or anything else in my life.
I have never had tuberculosis, and as far as I know, I have never been exposed to anyone with it.
A couple of coworkers sharing our open-plan office have been coughing with a mild bug over the past two weeks.
I work as a software designer in an office, so I am not exposed to industrial dust, toxic fumes, mold, or birds.
I do not have asthma, eczema, seasonal allergies, or allergic rhinitis.
I have had a mild dull headache, slight ear fullness, and all-over muscle fatigue since this illness began.
I tried some over-the-counter acetaminophen and cold tablets for a couple of days, but they did not help the cough, and I have not taken any antibiotics.

I thought I just caught that lingering dry cough everyone at my office has been passing around. I'm worried this hacking cough will ruin my client presentations next week and make a terrible impression on my boss.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications or herbal supplements right now.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I only drink one or two beers on weekend social occasions, and never heavily.
I live alone in a residential apartment and work full-time in an IT office.
Both of my parents are healthy with mild high blood pressure, and there is no family history of asthma or lung problems.

exam.finding: Young man appearing mildly fatigued with intermittent dry coughing, in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Both tympanic membranes are clear with normal light reflexes and no erythema, fluid, or bullae.
Nasal mucosa is pink without rhinorrhea; posterior pharynx shows mild erythema without exudates or cobblestoning.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Percussion is resonant bilaterally across all lung fields without localized dullness.
Diffuse faint expiratory wheezes and scattered fine end-inspiratory crackles heard bilaterally; no bronchial breathing.
Regular rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, no audible murmurs or rubs.
No digital clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema noted on bilateral lower extremities.
